I believe it can. Money today functions primarily as a metric of demand. An anonymous (though not so much anymore) medium of communicating demand. And it also functions 'mechanically'. Figuratively speaking, a token to put in a slot and make the vending machine go. But in our digitally networked civilization we can quantify costs and measure demand through consumption more directly and accurately than ever before and apply predictive quantitative analysis to it. This is what futurist Jacque Fresco refers to as a 'resource base economy'. You don't need a separate medium of exchange if you understand the relative demand/value of resources and can track their flow. You don't even need to track it that 'deeply' --ie, down to every purchase of every product (though you would for that sake of their 'spimes', but that's another discussion)-- if you can predict the resource demand accurately a bit higher up the production food chain. And so this is how Fresco--and many other futurists--arrive at a vision of a moneyless future where goods are 'free within reason' and you can simply walk into a store and take what goods you want off the shelf. And this can work because human beings aren't the imaginary homo economicus economists pretend we are. We are not compelled to behave like kids locked in a candy store overnight. Indeed, this has to work because, with the help of automation and artificial intelligence, profit is being mathematically factored out of the market.

In the absence coercion and monopoly, all profit is based on a divergence in the perception of value. On one party in an exchange having a different idea of the value of something compared to the other party. In a truly transparent economy that difference would not be possible, and so everything would be down to profitless barter. You would have a rush to the bottom in price capitulation. And as we increasingly digitize our markets we are, at the same time, making them more transparent. Mathematically whittling away at the hidden factors of cost through quantitative analysis. Mathematically factoring out the difference in the perception of value and thus profit and driving a rush to the bottom. So increasingly large amounts of money zoom ever faster around the globe electronically in search of smaller more transitory 'spot market bargains'. It's becoming really hard now to hide why something has a particular price in one place as opposed to another, and so commodity prices now tend to globally capitulate. The machines now know and respond to the market better than any human can. So we are left with only one commodity whose value has, deliberately, never been 'scientifically' quantified and so becomes the primary basis of obfuscation and profit; labor. And manipulation of labor value through globalization is the game business has played since the '70s, suppressing wage growth because that's now where all the profit comes from.

But now automation is making labor just as finely quantifiable as everything else. If a robot does a job, the cost of doing that job becomes concrete, predictable, uniform and the true cost of what it produces that much harder to obfuscate. And we know robot labor value it's always declining, because the technology is always being refined. Robots will never get more expensive. With automation you can't manipulate and exploit the social, cultural, and political factors that create global variations in labor value. Labor becomes a commodity with a globally capitulating, steadily declining, price like everything else. So if everyone has machines/math that will tell them exactly what the cost/value of everything is supposed to be, how do you turn a profit? Impose a 'convention' on the margin? In retail there's a convention of a roughly 30% 'fair' markup. But no one really sticks to that rule. There's no one enforcing it. If there's little competition, that percentage goes up. If there a lot of competition, that goes down and you get a 'price war' that drives price to cost. What product in the world today has no competition? (which explains why corporations today are obsessed with control of 'intellectual property' because the basis of a margin on value is shifting toward design novelty) This is the 'crisis of Capitalism' we often hear about but which isn't often explained. This is how technology is eroding the paradigms of the Industrial Age from the inside.

So we come to the oft-mischaracterized idea of Universal Basic Income. Many think this is some kind of alternative to welfare. No. It's about what you do when the traditional concepts of profit and labor stop making sense, but, somehow, civilization still has to work. (and there really isn't very much preventing angry mobs from burning the mansions to the ground...) If your machines have 'total economic awareness' you can predict what the 'overhead' of any given standard of living is. So society has an option to concretely define a baseline for everyone, establish its cost, and code the networks of production to supply it. Profit doesn't work as an incentive anymore. As long as you have automation and AI pushing ever-better quantitative analysis, you have a lemming rush to the bottom. There's no getting around that. So something else has to make things go. Logically, need is all you need. Base an economy on demand and social capital and you'll get a different sort of rush to the top. A maximizing of the baseline standard of living driven by another incentive; love and honor. That's really what motivates the capitalists anyway. Money is the obsession of peasants.
